title: ～ば～のに — if only ～, then ～ (regret)
summary: Expresses regret or dissatisfaction about a situation that did not turn out as hoped: “if only ～, I could ～.” The first half is the ば-form condition, and the second half ends with のに. It is used for the present and the past.

patterns.gloss: present counterfactual: あれば、できるのに (if I had it, I could)

patterns.form: ば形 ＋ 〜たのに（過去の反対）
patterns.gloss: past counterfactual: 勉強すれば、合格できたのに

body.p: The condition is not true, and the speaker feels that is a pity: お金があれば旅行できるのに means “I have no money, so I can't travel.” The のに at the end carries the complaint or regret and leaves the sentence open.
For the present, the ending is the present form (できるのに). For the past, it is the past form (できたのに). Because it can sound like blame when aimed at someone (電話をくれれば…迎えに行ったのに), use it carefully.

examples.ja: お金（かね）があれば、旅行（りょこう）できるのに。
examples.romaji: Okane ga areba, ryokō dekiru noni.
examples.tr: If only I had money, I could travel.

examples.ja: もっと勉強（べんきょう）すれば、合格（ごうかく）できたのに。
examples.romaji: Motto benkyō sureba, gōkaku dekita noni.
examples.tr: If only you had studied more, you could have passed.

examples.ja: 電話（でんわ）をくれれば、駅（えき）まで迎（むか）えに行（い）ったのに。
examples.romaji: Denwa o kurereba, eki made mukae ni itta noni.
examples.tr: If only you had called, I would have gone to pick you up at the station.

pitfalls: The ending のに here is regret, not the “although” の に in the middle of a sentence. Do not add a main verb after it.
Not for real, still-possible conditions. For those, use ～ば～ます (If you do, ...).
